name: Morphea (Localized Scleroderma)

criteria.description: Presence of one or more well-demarcated sclerotic plaques with ivory or waxy appearance
Localized skin thickening and induration without systemic involvement
Skin biopsy showing dermal sclerosis with thickened collagen bundles and loss of adnexal structures
No clinical or laboratory evidence of systemic sclerosis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: At least two major criteria including clinical plaques and localized skin thickening, plus absence of systemic sclerosis features
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Histopathology is supportive but not mandatory if clinical features are typical

pathognomonic.notes: Typically well-demarcated with a shiny surface

searchTerms: light or dark spots within plaques

common.symptomName: Mild pain or tenderness in lesions
searchTerms: mild pain or soreness in lesions

common.symptomName: Restricted joint movement adjacent to plaques
searchTerms: joint stiffness adjacent to skin lesions

occasional.symptomName: Subcutaneous tissue involvement causing deep induration
searchTerms: deep skin and fat tissue hardening
limited joint flexibility due to fibrosis

occasional.symptomName: Mild limb asymmetry due to tissue atrophy
searchTerms: mild limb size difference from tissue loss
slight asymmetry of arms or legs
unequal limb size due to atrophy

rare.symptomName: Neuropathic pain or paresthesia near lesions
searchTerms: nerve pain or tingling near lesions
burning or numbness near affected skin

rare.symptomName: Ocular involvement (e.g. uveitis) in linear morphea
searchTerms: eye inflammation linked to skin disease
uveitis or eye irritation in morphea
reduced muscle strength adjacent to lesions
weak muscles close to affected skin

rare.symptomName: Systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss
searchTerms: systemic signs like chills and losing weight

laboratory: Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP)
Autoantibodies usually negative or low titer ANA
Absence of systemic sclerosis-specific antibodies (e.g. anti-Scl-70, anti-centromere)
imaging: MRI may show dermal and subcutaneous thickening
Ultrasound can detect skin and soft tissue fibrosis
genetic: No specific genetic markers identified; possible HLA associations
other: Skin biopsy demonstrating thickened collagen bundles and loss of adnexal structures

distinguishingFeatures: Predominantly affects genital and perianal skin
Histopathology shows epidermal thinning and basal cell degeneration
Malignant skin tumor with infiltrative growth

redFlags: Rapid progression of skin thickening beyond localized plaques
Development of systemic symptoms (e.g. Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia)
Neurological deficits or seizures in linear morphea involving the face/scalp
references: Mertens JS et al. Morphea: Clinical and Pathological Features. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2020.
Fett N, Werth VP. Update on morphea: part I. Epidemiology, clinical presentation, and pathogenesis. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2011.
Kreuter A et al. Morphea: Current Concepts and Treatment Options. Am J Clin Dermatol. 2012.
